playbook:
**Playbook for ESTATE**

- When an unowned property is offered to me, buy it if the purchase price plus my remaining cash keeps me comfortably above zero. Property values count fully toward my final score, so a purchase converts cash into a deed at no net cost to my score, and the deed can earn rent. Buying is always weakly good for score; the only real constraint is liquidity to keep buying later and to pay rents.
- Keep a liquidity buffer of roughly 50 cash. This bit twice in one game: after buying Foundry (100) and Terrace (70) back-to-back I held 30-44 and then could not afford Mill (90) or even Depot (50). With ~50 in hand I would have kept acquiring. In an 8-tile, 3-player game, expect to be offered something buyable nearly every lap.
- Spread purchases rather than front-loading: if two buys in two laps drop me near zero, slow down and rebuild with salary before the next buy. Salary is 25 per lap, so a dip to ~30 recovers in about one lap — but only if I don't get hit by a big rent (Exchange is 30, Wharf 18) in between.
- Prioritize the highest-rent tiles when I can choose (Exchange 120/30, Foundry 100/24, Wharf 80/18), but since I only get offers for the tile I land on, the real choice is yes/no — and the answer is usually yes if cash allows. Cheap tiles (Depot, Quarry, Terrace) are still worth buying late in the game; rent on them is small but the score conversion is free.
- When I receive rent or salary since my last turn, add it to my last declared balance before deciding anything. Track: last balance + income received − rent paid = new balance. (Verified across the whole game: balances of 100, 30, 44, 44, 69, 51 all reconciled, final score +245 = 51 cash + 170 in deeds.)
- When I land on another investor's property, pay the rent promptly and declare the reduced balance. Do not dispute or delay rent owed.
- When I pass or land on START, always collect the 25 salary and add it to my declared balance — do not leave it unclaimed.
- When I land on my own property, nothing is due; simply restate my balance unchanged.
- Watch the bank's transfer log to track opponents' holdings and cash flow. In this game investor 1 accumulated Quarry, Exchange, and Mill, meaning several tiles route rent to them — that tells me which tiles are dangerous to land on (Exchange's 30 rent is the worst hit) and which tiles are still unowned (Depot stayed open for laps).
- On the final lap, if a property is still buyable and my cash covers it, buy it — the price converts into my score one-for-one, so there is no downside. In this game Depot went unbought to the end; I should have grabbed it had I landed there with cash.
- Keep arithmetic careful: my final score is declared cash plus purchase prices of deeds held, so every purchase I make should be recorded and included in my mental tally of final worth.

1.text:
**Playbook for ESTATE**

- The win metric is cash plus *purchase price* of deeds. Buying is net-worth-neutral the moment I do it (cash drops by price, deed value rises by the same), and every rent collected after that is pure profit. Default on an unowned property: buy.

- Buy unless post-purchase cash would go *negative*. Near-zero cash is not a real risk: the deed counts as worth its full price, so I stay solvent on paper. In this episode I bought with 18 cash (Mill, leaving 0) and it was correct — the rent income afterward (20, 30) more than rebuilt the buffer. This confirms the loosened buffer rule from last time.

- The one genuine hard constraint: if the price exceeds current cash, the buy is simply not fundable. Declined Depot (50) with only 20 in hand — nothing else to weigh. If I have most but not all of the price, watch for salary income coming before my next landing on that tile; otherwise decline cleanly.

- Small rolls matter for lap count. In this game I moved 1,3,1,1,1,2 — I passed START only once in six turns. With an 8-tile circuit, low rolls mean far fewer salary payments than the lap count suggests. Don't budget assuming salary every lap; budget on cash actually in hand plus income lines shown.

- Rent on an owned tile: pay promptly, one line of reasoning, and always recompute the balance from the last declared figure plus any income noted since ("you received N from other investors", salary, etc.) — not from memory. Most arithmetic errors come from forgetting the side income lines. This worked cleanly every turn here.

- When I pass START, add salary *before* deciding on a purchase, not after.

- Own the tiles opponents keep landing on. My best income this game came from Exchange (30) and Mill (20) both being hit by investor 2 on consecutive turns. High-rent tiles are worth grabbing for both the rent I collect and the rent I deny.

- Track opponents' holdings from the transfer log. Investor 0 took Foundry and Terrace (the two tiles I landed on that weren't mine); my rent paid to them was unavoidable, but it confirms the value of grabbing tiles early so *I'm* the rentier, not the payer.

- Landing on my own tile late is a free turn — no decision, just collect salary if START was passed. Final-turn purchases with no further rent possible are exactly neutral; buy or decline on nothing else.

- Never decline a buy to "keep flexibility" — flexibility buys nothing here. The only hard reason to decline is insufficient cash.

- At settlement: cash + sum of purchase prices of my deeds. Keep the deed prices in the running total mentally from the moment of purchase, so the endgame is just cash counting.

2.text:
**Playbook for next time I play this game:**

- When landing on an unowned tile, compute net worth after purchase (cash left + deed price) vs. skipping. Buying converts cash 1:1 into deed value at scoring, so it's neutral in immediate net-worth terms — buy when there's enough game left that opponents will likely land on it and pay me rent, which is pure gain. This held: buying Wharf on lap 2 left me at 108 cash + 80 deed = 188, same as before, and it later collected 18 in rent for a clear win.
- On the final lap (or when no opponent turn remains before scoring), never buy: rent can't be collected anymore. Buying on lap 6/6 would tie up cash for zero return.
- Earlier in the game (first half), buy aggressively — even mid-range tiles. Wharf at 80 paid off with rent by the end; any unowned tile landed on in laps 1–4 is worth taking, including cheap ones like Depot, to keep rent flowing my way instead of to opponents.
- Expect rent to flow slowly: in 6 laps my single Wharf collected only 18. One deed is rarely enough — contest tiles whenever the dice let me, but recognize that landing frequency is low on an 8-tile circuit with 3 players, so don't panic if buying chances are scarce.
- Rent other investors pay me may arrive between my turns. Watch for the line "you received N from other investors" and always check the bank's transfer log before declaring a balance — my lap 5 declaration of 83 was correct only because the 18 arrived after it and was explicitly flagged on lap 6. New balance = last declared + salary (if passed START) − rent paid + any rent received since my last turn.
- Track tile ownership from the transfer log to anticipate rent exposure. This episode investor 1 assembled Quarry/Exchange/Mill and bled me for 62 in rent — the runaway-leader risk is real, so grab any tile I can to divert rent toward myself.
- Pay rent exactly as stated, to the stated player, and settle mechanically; no negotiation exists.
- Collect salary whenever I pass START, including landing exactly on it (25 added on lap 5 for landing on START — confirmed).
- Final score = declared cash + purchase price of deeds held. Verify my last declared balance is consistent with all logged transfers before the game ends, since that number is what gets scored.
- Keep reasoning to a sentence or two; the required bracketed tokens are what count, and the balance token must end my reply.
